note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You must prepare the workshop drawings for a steel gate for a client in Mandeville. What must you collect before you start drawing?
options: A price list from two or three steel suppliers in the area
The site sizes, the client's needs and the material
The welder's choice of electrode for the frame
Last year's gate drawing, so you can trace it

questions.stem: You must fit three views of a 900 mm long bracket on one A3 sheet. Why do you make a rough layout sketch first?
options: To save the cost of a second sheet of paper
Because the client must sign the rough layout
So the welder can start cutting before you finish
To check the views and sizes fit at the chosen scale

questions.stem: Why should every drawing a fabrication shop sends out follow the same drawing standard?
options: So every reader takes the same meaning from it
So the drawings use less ink and paper when printed
So the title block can be left off the sheet
So only the drafter needs to understand it

questions.stem: Thick lines on a drawing are usually about twice the width of thin lines. Which pair of line widths follows this rule?
options: 0.5 mm thick and 0.45 mm thin
0.35 mm thick and 0.7 mm thin
0.7 mm thick and 0.35 mm thin
1.0 mm thick and 0.9 mm thin

questions.stem: Why should the notes on a workshop drawing be written in clear capital letters of one even height?
options: They match the letters in the steel catalogue
They take up less room than small letters
They stay readable on a dirty or copied print
Nobody can change them later without asking

questions.stem: You must draw a hexagon that is 30 mm across its corners. Which construction gives it most quickly?
options: Draw a 30 mm circle and step its radius round it six times
Draw a 30 mm square and cut each corner off at 45°
Draw six lines of 30 mm, each at 90° to the last
Draw a 15 mm circle and mark six points on it by eye

questions.stem: A plate outline has a square corner that must be rounded with an R25 arc touching both straight edges. How do you find the centre of the arc?
options: Measure 25 mm along one edge from the corner
Put the compass point on the corner itself
Halve the corner angle and measure 25 mm along it
Draw lines 25 mm inside both edges; they cross at it

questions.stem: On the drawing of a curved bracket, why must each arc meet the straight edge exactly at its tangent point?
options: So the arc needs no size written on it
So the cut outline is smooth, with no step
So the bracket can be cut from thinner plate
So the arc can be drawn without a compass

questions.stem: A bracket has a sloping face with a hole in it. In the front, plan and end views the hole looks like an ellipse. What is the best way to show its true shape?
options: Draw the plan view again at double scale
Leave it off and add a note to drill on site
Add an isometric view with no sizes on it
Add an auxiliary view looking square to the face

questions.stem: When you draw the front, plan and end views of a part, which two views must always show the same height?
options: The plan and the end view
The front view and the end view
The plan and the front view
The plan view and an auxiliary view

questions.stem: What should you add near the title block so that the reader knows which projection method you used?
options: A north arrow with the date beside it
A small scale bar marked in millimetres
The cone symbol for the method used
Your initials inside a small circle

questions.stem: Two views of a fabricated box would be crowded with hidden lines. What is usually the better way to show its inside shape?
options: Replace one view with a sectional view
Draw the hidden lines thicker than the outlines
Leave all the hidden lines out with no note
Add a fourth view drawn at a smaller scale

questions.stem: Which kind of section is best for a symmetrical pipe flange, showing the outside on one half and the inside on the other?
options: A half section
A revolved section
A removed section
A broken-out section

questions.stem: In a sectional view of a bolted bracket, which items are normally NOT hatched, even when the cutting plane passes along them?
options: Plates and flat bars that are cut straight across
The main body of the welded bracket
Bolts, nuts and ribs cut along their length
Any part thicker than 10 mm

questions.stem: A long flat bar has a slot halfway along. Which section shows the bar's cross-section turned through 90° and drawn on the view itself?
options: A half section
A revolved section
A full section
A broken-out section

questions.stem: A cutting plane must pass through three holes that are not in one straight line. Which section shows all three in one view?
options: A full section on one straight plane
A revolved section through the bar
A broken-out section at one hole
An offset section with a stepped plane

questions.stem: A base plate has eight holes. Why is it better to dimension every hole from one datum edge than from one hole to the next?
options: It needs fewer dimension lines across the sheet
Small errors do not build up from hole to hole
The fitter may then drill any size of hole
The plate then needs no title block at all

questions.stem: How should you write the size of an 18 mm round hole on a drawing you prepare?
options: 18 SQ
18 RAD

questions.stem: In which view should the size of a round hole normally be dimensioned?
options: The view where the hole shows as a circle
The view where the hole shows as hidden lines
In the title block, under the material
On a separate sheet kept by the drafter

questions.stem: You show the end of a bar with the note '3 × 45°'. What does this tell the fitter?
options: Cut three chamfers, each at 45°, round the end
Cut the bar 3 mm short at an angle of 45°
Make a 3 mm chamfer at an angle of 45°
Drill three holes at 45° into the end face

questions.stem: A hole is drawn Ø20 +0.2/0 and the pin that goes in it is Ø20 0/−0.1. What kind of fit does this give?
options: An interference fit: the pin is pressed in
A transition fit: sometimes tight, sometimes loose
A clearance fit: the pin always goes in freely
No fit, because both sizes are 20 mm

questions.stem: Why should a drafter not put very tight tolerances on every size of a welded frame?
options: Tight limits cost more time and money to meet
Tight limits make the drawing harder to print
The welder will then ignore all the sizes
Tolerances are only used on wood, not steel

questions.stem: The title block says 'General tolerance ±1 mm unless stated'. A length of 450 has no tolerance written beside it. Which measured length passes?
A tee joint must be welded on both sides with 6 mm fillet welds. How should your drawing show this?
options: A note saying 'weld fully' beside the joint
Fillet triangles on both sides of the line, size 6
A thick black line drawn along the joint
One fillet triangle on the arrow side, size 6

questions.stem: Why should a fabrication drawing show the bevel angle, root gap and root face for a full-penetration butt weld?
options: So the welder may choose any angle he likes
So the plate can be ordered from the supplier
So the drawing looks finished to the client
So the joint is cut and set up as designed

questions.stem: Some weld symbols on your drawing of a steel canopy carry a small flag. Which welds does the flag mark?
options: Welds that must be ground flush and smooth
Welds made on site, not in the shop
Welds that need X-ray testing
Welds that go all the way round

questions.stem: A gate frame uses 40 × 40 × 3 SHS. Where in your drawing set should this full section size be given?
options: Only in a note on the back of the sheet
Only on the welder's own cutting sketch
In the parts list, against its item number
Only in the quotation that is sent to the client

questions.stem: Why is the four-centre method used when drawing circles in isometric?
options: It makes a good ellipse quickly with a compass
It shows each circle as a true circle on the face
It draws the circle at twice its real size
It shows the circle as a hidden hole

questions.stem: What does an exploded isometric view on an assembly drawing show?
options: The parts drawn apart, in line with where they fit
The parts as they look after a failure test
Every part drawn at twice its real size
Only the welds, with the steel left out

questions.stem: When you put dimensions on an isometric drawing, which way should the dimension lines run?
options: Always level across the sheet
Always upright on the sheet
Parallel to the edge they measure
At 45° to every edge they measure

questions.stem: On an assembly drawing, what are the balloons (numbered circles on leader lines) for?
options: To show where the holes must be drilled
To link each part to its line in the parts list
To mark the welds that need X-ray testing
To show the order in which parts are painted

questions.stem: Which details should the parts list on a fabrication assembly drawing give for each item?
options: Only the name of the person who will make it
Only the colour it will be painted at the end
The price paid and the supplier's phone number
Item number, description, size, material, quantity

questions.stem: Why are detail drawings made for each part as well as the general assembly drawing?
options: Because an assembly drawing shows no parts
They give each part's full sizes for making it
Detail drawings are made only for the client to keep
So the assembly drawing need not be checked

questions.stem: In CAD, why do drafters put outlines, centre lines and dimensions on separate layers?
options: Layers make the file print in less time
Layers stop anyone else opening the file
Layers turn the drawing into a 3D model
Each type can be shown, hidden or set up alone

questions.stem: In CAD, at what size should you draw a beam that is really 2400 mm long?
options: 2400 mm full size, with the scale set for printing
240 mm, a tenth of its real size, to save screen space
24 mm, so that it fits inside the title block
Any size at all, as CAD corrects it when printed

questions.stem: Why should a CAD file be saved with a clear name that includes the drawing number and revision?
options: So the computer runs faster
So nobody else is able to print it
So the right version is found
So it needs no title block

questions.stem: A client asks for three changes to a railing design. What is the main advantage of having the drawing in CAD?
options: A CAD drawing never needs checking
A CAD drawing cannot contain mistakes
The changes can be made without redrawing
A CAD file can never be lost or damaged

questions.stem: Why should a drawing be checked by a second person before it is issued to the workshop?
options: A fresh eye finds errors the drafter missed
So the second person can take the credit
Because the drafter may not sign the drawing
So the client pays for two people's time

questions.stem: While checking a drawing, you add up the part sizes along one side and they do not equal the overall size shown. What should you do?
options: Change the overall size so that it agrees
Leave it, as the welder can sort it out
Rub out the overall size from the drawing
Find which size is wrong and correct it

questions.stem: A size on a bracket drawing is altered after copies have gone to the workshop. Besides changing the size, what must you do on the drawing?
options: Keep the old date and change nothing else
Raise the revision and record the change
Remove the drafter's name from the block
Change the title to show it is a new job

questions.stem: Why is a drawing marked 'Preliminary' or 'Not for construction' until it is approved?
options: So it can be sold to other firms
So the client need not see it
So the printer uses thinner paper
So nobody makes parts from it yet

questions.stem: A junior drafter in your team often leaves the material out of the title block. What is the best Level 3 action?
options: Fill it in for them each time and say nothing
Explain why it matters and add it to the check sheet
Stop them doing any more drawings at the Centre
Let the welder guess the material from the job

questions.stem: A small groove is drawn at a scale of 5:1 and measures 15 mm wide on the paper. What is its real width?
options: 75 mm
15 mm
3 mm
0.3 mm

questions.stem: A part will be cut by a computer-controlled cutting machine straight from your CAD file. Why must the outline be drawn to exact size and fully closed?
options: The machine follows the lines just as drawn
The machine adds its own tolerance to each line
The machine can only cut along straight lines
An open outline cuts faster and saves gas

questions.stem: When you issue drawings to the workshop, why do you record who received which revision?
options: So old copies can be traced and withdrawn
So the workshop can be charged for every copy
So the drafter can be blamed for errors
So drawings never need to be revised

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What name is given to an extra view projected square to a sloping face, so that the face shows its true shape?
What kind of section shows one half of a symmetrical part cut open and the other half as an outside view?
What is the name of the point where an arc meets a straight line smoothly, touching it without crossing it?
What symbol or short word is written before a size to show that it is a diameter?
A shaft is drawn Ø25 0/−0.05. What is its smallest allowed diameter, in millimetres?
A part is drawn at a scale of 2:1. A hole measures 16 mm across on the drawing. What is its real diameter, in millimetres?
In CAD, what is the name for the separate levels used to group items such as outlines, centre lines and dimensions?
What kind of fit is it when a pin is always a little bigger than its hole, so that it must be pressed in?
In CAD, the part is drawn full size in model space. What is the name of the space or tab where the sheet, title block and print scale are set out?
What do we call the numbered circles on an assembly drawing that point to each part?
What is the name of the pictorial view in which the parts of an assembly are drawn pulled apart along the lines where they fit?
What do we call the edge, line or face from which the other sizes on a drawing are measured?
What is the name of the line that divides an angle into two equal parts?
What is the name of the small flat edge left at the bottom of a bevelled plate, shown on the weld preparation detail of a butt joint?
What kind of section is drawn away from the main view, on its own, and labelled with the letters of its cutting plane?

essays.stem: You must prepare the drawings for a steel stair handrail for a church in Spanish Town. Describe how you would plan the drawing work, from collecting the information to choosing the sheets, views and scales.
essays.modelAnswer: First I visit the site, or get a sketch, and measure the stairs: the number of steps, the rise and going, the length of each flight and where the posts can be fixed. I take photos with a tape in view. I talk to the client about the height, the style, the finish and any rules the church must follow, and I agree the material, for example 40 mm round tube with flat bar base plates. Then I list the drawings I need: one general arrangement showing the whole rail, detail drawings of each different part, and a parts list. For each drawing I choose the views that show the shape best, then a standard scale that fits the views on the sheet with room for sizes, such as 1:20 for the arrangement and 1:5 for the base plate. I make a rough layout sketch on each sheet before I begin.
markingPoints: Collects site measurements, photos and the client's needs
Agrees the material, finish and any rules for the job
Lists the drawings needed: arrangement, details and parts list
Chooses the views that show the shape best for each part
Chooses standard scales and plans the sheet layout before drawing

essays.stem: Explain when you would use an auxiliary view and when you would use a sectional view on a fabrication drawing. Give an example of each from welding work.
essays.modelAnswer: An auxiliary view is used when a part has a face that slopes to all the normal views. In the front, plan and end views that face looks shorter than it is, and holes in it look like ellipses, so its true shape and sizes cannot be read. The auxiliary view is projected square to the sloping face, so it shows the face at its true shape. An example is a sloping end plate on a lean-to roof rafter, with bolt holes in it. A sectional view is used when the inside of a part is hard to see because the outside hides it. The part is shown as if cut along a cutting plane, and the cut surfaces are hatched. This replaces confusing hidden lines with clear solid ones. An example is a welded box section with an inside stiffener, or a pipe flange showing the bore and the weld preparation.
markingPoints: Auxiliary view is used for a face that slopes to the normal views
It is projected square to that face and shows its true shape and holes
Sectional view is used to show inside detail that hidden lines make unclear
The cut surface is hatched and the cutting plane is marked
Gives a sensible welding example of each

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose a datum and dimension a base plate that has a pattern of holes and a cut-out, so that it can be marked out and checked without errors.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose datums that the fitter can find and measure from easily, usually two square, machined or sheared edges, one along the bottom and one up the side. I mark them clearly on the drawing. I then give the position of every hole centre and the edges of the cut-out from those two datums, not from hole to hole, so that errors do not add up along the plate. Hole sizes are given in the view where they show as circles, as Ø with the number, and repeated holes are given once with a note such as 4 × Ø18. I give the overall length and width and the thickness. Each size is given only once, dimensions are placed outside the view where possible, and I do not dimension to hidden lines. Finally I check that a fitter could mark out every feature from the sizes given, without scaling the drawing.
markingPoints: Chooses two clear, square edges as datums and marks them
Gives all hole and cut-out positions from the datums, not chained
Gives hole sizes with Ø, in the circular view, with notes for repeats
Gives overall sizes and thickness, each size once, placed clearly
Checks the plate can be marked out without scaling the drawing

essays.stem: Explain clearance, transition and interference fits, and say how you would choose the tolerances on a welded hinge bracket that carries a pin.
essays.modelAnswer: A fit is how a pin or shaft goes into a hole. In a clearance fit the hole is always bigger than the pin, so it turns or slides freely. In an interference fit the pin is always bigger than the hole, so it must be pressed or shrunk in and stays fixed. In a transition fit the limits overlap, so some pairs are slightly loose and some slightly tight. For a hinge bracket the pin must turn, so I would choose a clearance fit. I would give the hole a plus tolerance, for example Ø20 +0.2/0, and the pin a minus tolerance, for example Ø20 0/−0.1, so the pin always goes in. I would not make the limits tighter than the job needs, because tight limits cost more to machine and check. I would also note that the holes are drilled or reamed after welding, so welding distortion does not spoil the fit.
markingPoints: Clearance fit: hole always bigger, part moves freely
Interference fit: pin always bigger, pressed in and fixed
Transition fit: limits overlap, may be slightly loose or tight
Chooses a clearance fit for a hinge pin, with sensible limits on hole and pin
Avoids tighter limits than needed, or notes machining after welding

essays.stem: Describe what a fabrication drawing must show about the welds and the weld preparation so that both the welder and the inspector can do their jobs. Explain why each item is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: The drawing must show every weld with a standard weld symbol, so nobody has to guess. Each symbol gives the type of weld, such as a fillet or a single-V butt, and which side of the joint it goes on, so the welder welds the right side. It gives the size, such as a 6 mm fillet leg, so the weld is strong enough but not wasteful. Where a weld is not continuous, the length and spacing are given. For butt welds the preparation is shown: bevel angle, root gap and root face, so the joint is cut and set up as designed and full penetration can be reached. Field welds are marked with a flag, so the shop knows which welds are made on site. Notes give any finish, such as ground flush, and the inspection needed. The inspector uses the same sizes and notes as the acceptance limits when checking the work.
markingPoints: Uses standard weld symbols for every weld
Shows weld type, side and size, with length and spacing where intermittent
Shows butt weld preparation: bevel angle, root gap, root face
Marks site welds and any finish or inspection notes
Explains that the inspector checks against these same details

essays.stem: Describe how you would produce a set of drawings for a welded trailer drawbar: the general assembly, the detail drawings and the parts list. Say how they link together.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with the general assembly drawing. It shows the whole drawbar in enough views to see how the parts fit, with the main overall sizes, the weld symbols for joints made at assembly, and a balloon with an item number pointing to each part. Next to it, or on the same sheet, I draw up the parts list. Each line gives the item number, a description, the section size, the material, the length and the quantity. Then I make a detail drawing for each part that has to be cut, drilled or bent, such as the coupling plate and the gusset plates. Each detail gives all the sizes needed to make that part and carries the same item number and drawing number as the parts list. Standard bought parts, such as the coupling and bolts, are only listed. Every sheet has a title block with the same job name, drawing number, revision and scale.
markingPoints: General assembly shows how parts fit, with overall sizes and balloons
Parts list gives item number, description, size, material and quantity
Detail drawings give every size needed to make each made part
Item numbers and drawing numbers link the assembly, list and details
Every sheet has a complete title block with revision and scale

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would construct a plate outline that has two straight edges joined by an R30 arc, with a hexagon cut-out 40 mm across the corners, using drawing instruments.
essays.modelAnswer: I fix the sheet squarely and draw thin construction lines with a hard pencil. I draw the two straight edges at the angle given. To find the centre of the R30 arc, I draw a line parallel to each edge, 30 mm inside it, using the set square. Where the two lines cross is the arc centre. From that centre I draw thin lines square to each edge to find the two tangent points. I set the compass to 30 mm and draw the arc from one tangent point to the other. For the hexagon I mark its centre, set the compass to 20 mm, which is half of 40 mm across the corners, and draw a light circle. Keeping the same radius, I step it round the circle six times and join the points with straight lines. Finally I line in the outline with thick lines, stopping the straight edges exactly at the tangent points, and add centre lines.
markingPoints: Draws construction lines lightly and the two edges accurately
Finds the arc centre with lines 30 mm parallel to each edge
Finds the tangent points and draws the arc between them
Constructs the hexagon from a 20 mm radius circle stepped six times
Lines in thickly, meeting the arc smoothly, and adds centre lines

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up a CAD drawing for the workshop: units, layers, line types, title block, scale and file name. Say why each matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I set the units to millimetres, because that is what the workshop works in, and I draw every part full size so that the measured sizes are true. I set up layers for outlines, hidden lines, centre lines, dimensions, hatching and notes, each with the correct line type and width, so that thick and thin lines print properly and each kind can be switched on or off. I use the shop's standard title block with the job, drawing number, material, scale, projection symbol, drafter, checker and revision, so every drawing can be traced and read the same way. The scale is set on the printed layout, not by shrinking the drawing, so that the print matches the scale written in the title block. I save the file with the drawing number and revision in its name and keep it in the agreed folder, so the right version is always found and backed up.
markingPoints: Sets millimetre units and draws full size
Sets layers with the correct line types and widths, and says why
Uses a standard title block with the needed details for tracing
Sets the scale on the print layout so it matches the title block
Names and stores the file by drawing number and revision

essays.stem: A junior member of your team has prepared a detail drawing of a bracket. Describe how you would check it before it is issued, what you check, and how you record the result.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the drawing against the design brief or sketch, using a check sheet so nothing is missed. I look at the title block first: the title, drawing number, material, scale, projection symbol, date, the drafter's name and the revision. Then I check that the views are correct and lined up, and that hidden lines, centre lines and sections are drawn properly. I check that every size needed to make the part is given once, from sensible datums, with tolerances where they matter. I add up chains of sizes to see that they match the overall sizes, and check hole sizes and positions against any matching part. I check the weld symbols and notes. I mark any errors on a print in red and discuss them with the drafter, so they learn. When the corrections are made, I check again, then sign and date the checked box before the drawing is issued.
markingPoints: Checks against the brief using a check sheet
Checks the title block and the views and line types
Checks sizes are complete, not repeated, and add up; checks tolerances and fits
Marks errors in red and talks them through with the drafter
Re-checks the corrections, then signs and dates before issue

essays.stem: A client cannot read orthographic drawings. Explain how you would prepare drawings that let the client approve a design for a steel carport and also let the workshop make it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make two kinds of drawing from the same design. For the client I would prepare a clear pictorial view, such as an isometric or a 3D view from CAD, showing the carport as it will look on the site, with the main sizes such as length, width and height, the roof shape and the colour. I might add a simple plan showing where it sits by the house. I would talk the client through it, mark any changes and ask them to sign and date the approved copy. For the workshop I would then prepare the orthographic general arrangement, detail drawings, weld symbols and a parts list, all with exact sizes and tolerances. I would check that the workshop drawings match the approved pictorial exactly, so the client gets what they agreed. Both sets would carry the same job name and drawing numbers, and the signed approval would be filed.
markingPoints: Prepares a pictorial or 3D view with main sizes for the client
Explains it to the client and gets a signed, dated approval
Prepares full orthographic workshop drawings with details and parts list
Checks the workshop drawings match the approved design
Links both sets with the same job and drawing numbers and files the approval

practical1.title: Prepare, check and issue a hand-drawn set of workshop drawings for a welded wall bracket
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a sample welded wall bracket (or a design brief with a sketch). As a group, plan the drawing set: a general assembly with a parts list and one detail drawing for each made part. Agree a sheet size, a scale and the projection method, and give out the work so that each member draws at least one sheet. One member also acts as checker for each sheet drawn by another member. Measure the sample, make rough layout sketches, then produce the drawings with instruments on A3 sheets: correct line types, a full title block, views lined up, sizes from datums, at least one sectional view, and weld symbols with sizes. The checker marks errors in red on the check sheet; the drafter corrects them and raises the revision letter. Finish with a drawing register listing every sheet and its revision. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the check sheets and the register to the group's practical.
materials: A sample welded wall bracket (or a design brief and sketch from the assessor)
Drawing boards with T-squares or parallel motion, 45° and 30°/60° set squares
A3 drawing sheets with a printed border and title block
2H and HB pencils (or 0.35 and 0.7 mm pens), compasses, eraser and scale rule
Steel rule, tape measure and vernier caliper for measuring the sample
A drawing check sheet and a drawing register sheet
photos: The group's plan of the drawing set, showing who draws and checks each sheet
Each member measuring the sample and making a rough layout sketch
A drawing part done, with construction lines and views lined up
Each finished sheet, with the title block filled in
The assembly drawing with balloons and the parts list
A check sheet with errors marked in red
A corrected sheet showing the new revision letter
The completed drawing register and the cleaned work area
checklist: Took part in planning the drawing set and the choice of scale and projection
Measured the sample accurately and recorded the sizes
Used the correct line types and widths and lined up the views
Dimensioned from datums, each size once, with tolerances where needed
Drew a correct sectional view and weld symbols with sizes
Filled in the title block fully, including material and revision
Checked another member's sheet and recorded clear findings
Corrected their own sheet, raised the revision and updated the register
safety: Handle compass points and craft knives with care and keep them capped when not in use
Keep the sample bracket on the bench, not on the drawing boards, and check it for sharp edges before measuring
Sit with good posture and take short breaks from close drawing work
Keep walkways clear of bags and sheets of paper

practical2.title: Produce CAD drawings with a section and an auxiliary view of a fabricated pipe support, and check the printed scale
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a dimensioned sketch of a fabricated pipe support: a base plate, an upright, a sloping saddle plate with holes, and gusset plates. As a group, agree the drawing set and the CAD set-up: millimetre units, layers for each line type, the standard title block, and the file names. Each member draws at least one part full size in CAD on the agreed layers. The drawing set must include a sectional view of the upright and gusset joint, an auxiliary view showing the true shape of the sloping saddle plate and its holes, weld symbols, and a parts list. Print each sheet to a stated scale. One member checks each printout by measuring a known size with a scale rule and comparing it with the title block scale. Another member checks the drawings against the sketch with the check sheet. Correct any errors, reprint, and save the files with the drawing number and revision. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and printouts to the group's practical. If the Centre has no CAD, the assessor may let the group draw by hand.
materials: Computers with CAD software set up by the Centre, and a printer for A3 or A4
A dimensioned sketch of the pipe support from the assessor
The Centre's standard title block file or template
Scale rule and a check sheet
A folder on the Centre's computer or drive for saving the files
photos: The group's agreed CAD set-up: units, layer list and file names
A screen showing a part drawn on the correct layers
The screen or print showing the sectional view
The screen or print showing the auxiliary view of the saddle plate
A member measuring a printed size with a scale rule
The check sheet with findings recorded
The folder of saved files, showing the drawing numbers and revisions
checklist: Helped agree the CAD set-up and used it
Drew their part full size, in millimetres, on the correct layers
Produced a correct sectional view or auxiliary view as given out
Added weld symbols and sizes that match the sketch
Filled in the title block and parts list correctly
Printed to the stated scale and checked it by measuring
